name: Zoe Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead seven caption editors for a large media company that streams concerts and public events. Before a live feed, we check the speaker list and timing; during it, someone listens for mistakes that can confuse a viewer. I have an MBA and am good at keeping an editor calm when the feed changes without warning. I use an AI draft tool now and then, but an editor listens before a caption goes live.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home when the stream ends?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and live with Harun, who repairs bicycles for pay, and our children, nine and fifteen, in a mortgaged house. My manager wage is about typical, his repair fees vary, and we have three months of expenses saved. There are some other media offices nearby. Our daughter was in a school concert we streamed last month, which is why I remember one bad caption so clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small drafting tool is already here, and we still have a person watching each live caption feed. At the usual manager wage, Harun's repair income and three months of expenses in cash, our mortgage feels manageable. His bicycle shop has slow rainy weeks, though, so I still check the account before spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my seven caption editors to listen to the live audio before trusting a draft transcript. I'd tell the accessibility group we will keep the phone line for errors during an event. I would tell Harun the new tool can help with punctuation but not settle a complaint from a viewer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI now and then for a first draft, and I know its mistakes are usually ordinary words in the wrong place. My job still feels solid in a mild-change world, and there are a few other media offices within reach. I would not spend our three-month reserve on a clever upgrade for the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Tuesday I'll have the team replay the six live feeds with reported caption errors and correct the time stamps in the archive. Through the first plateau year I'll keep an editor on each live feed and use the current draft tool only after listening to the recording. I'll add 100 monthly to cash while my wage and Harun's paid repairs cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job. The errors still matter to viewers, and that gives us real work to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which error stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: During a school concert stream the caption said the hall was closing when the speaker said the hall was clapping. My daughter was in the audience and laughed, but a deaf grandparent missed the joke. A missing laugh can make a whole room look cold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep three months in cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bicycle shop pays by finished repair, not by the calendar. Our younger child is nine and the older fifteen, and school costs do not wait for a sunny cycling week. I would pause the extra 100 if mortgage or school costs needed it.

think: My job feels **solid** when AI changes little.

Save **100 monthly** only while wages and paid repairs cover mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Caption writing, timing, checking and answering accessibility complaints are almost all thinking work. Stronger AI could create a first pass so quickly that the company keeps fewer editors and perhaps one manager for several feeds. Harun still has to hold a bicycle wheel in his hands, but my desk changes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our accessibility group to test a hard live event, not only a clean studio recording. I'd ask the director to put an error limit and a named human escalation in writing before any staffing change. I'd tell my team what I know about the pilot, not promise their shifts are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be the manager cut when one person oversees several feeds. I can learn a tested tool, but occasional draft use has not taught me how to check a live automated caption stream. My pay covers most of our mortgage, and three months cash would go quickly if it stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'll ask the director for a paid two-event caption pilot, with the accessibility lead approving test cases and our editors checking every live line. If the pilot meets the agreed error limit and the director approves rollout, I'll bring its draft captions into our workflow while keeping a human escalation; I'll learn the monitoring screen with a senior editor on paid time first. I'll apply for posted accessibility manager jobs locally after checking pay and hours, keeping my current wage until a signed affordable offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the team's hours and mine. Testing it carefully may protect viewers, but it will also show how few editors the company thinks it needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which event would make a fair test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A live town meeting with overlapping speakers and a fire-alarm announcement. The word 'exit' cannot disappear because the system preferred a smoother sentence. I would ask the accessibility lead to score that case before anyone calls the pilot a success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep the error log private?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would show the editors and the director the same log, with names of viewers removed. People need to know whether the pilot passed before jobs are recounted. An error hidden in a report can still be heard by a viewer as silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 could understand speech, time captions and resolve complaints better than my team. My desk and the local accessibility desks would face the same change. Harun's physical bicycle repairs might still pay until capable robots arrive around 2031, though booking and estimates are thinking work that change in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my editors the 2028 date and ask for written notice terms. I'd tell Harun we should cancel the deposit on our summer music trip before the date is due. I'd tell viewers there must be a way to challenge a dangerous missing caption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my caption manager wage to end by 2028. Harun's repair income alone cannot pay the mortgage, and three months saved would vanish in a long search. I would lie awake wondering whether the children heard me say the trip was cancelled for the right reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask Harun to teach me basic chain and tyre repairs on two Saturdays using his shop tools, with another agreed adult looking after our younger child. I'd take additional paid customer repairs only if bookings exceed what Harun already handles and the extra receipts after parts pay for my time; I won't call shifting his existing work to me new income. We'll cancel the summer music-trip deposit before it is due this winter. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my caption wage ends, I'll apply for posted local jobs whose pay covers mortgage, food and school costs with Harun's confirmed profit, keeping my current wage until a signed offer if it still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I can learn a chain repair, but a booked customer cannot replace a full manager wage overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the shop support you through 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person can hold a wheel and change a tyre until capable robots do physical repairs around 2031; AGI can handle bookings and prices in 2028. Harun has tools and customers, but I do not know how many extra orders he can take. An extra repair only helps if somebody pays more than the parts cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How old would the children be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our younger child would be eleven and the older seventeen in 2028. The older may have study plans, but I won't invent a scholarship or a wage. Another adult would need to cover the younger one while both of us are working in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me learn what the shop really earns from an extra pair of hands while my caption wage still arrives. Caption management faces AGI in 2031, and even local media desks are thinking work. Harun's physical repairs could still need hands until capable robots arrive around 2034; booking and pricing face AGI in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my editors that the company needs a dated staffing plan before the caption desk shrinks. I'd tell Harun I want to see his parts bills and the shop's paid bookings before we talk about a second repair bench. I'd keep the accessibility complaint line open while I'm still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might earn some extra repair money if I can do safe work and Harun has more paid bookings than he can handle. I doubt it will match my manager wage; there are some local management vacancies, but their screen work could face AGI too. Five years lets me test actual shop demand without putting our mortgage cash into new equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'll take two additional booked repair afternoons each month under Harun's eye only when another agreed adult covers our younger child, his existing paid work is not displaced and net receipts after parts exceed the cost of my time. I'd save 150 monthly after mortgage and school costs while both incomes continue, pausing if the shop's paid bookings fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for posted local work only where a real wage with Harun's confirmed net repair income covers our bills; I'd keep taking extra repair orders only while paid demand exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own wage. Five years gives us time to see shop receipts, but a second pair of hands does not create customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair would you take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd replace a worn chain under Harun's supervision, then show the customer the old part and the new one. I don't yet know every brake system well enough to take a child's bicycle alone. A second set of hands is income only when there is a second bicycle at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy another repair stand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not out of our three-month reserve. I would first count the extra paid jobs across several months and price a stand against actual receipts. We have a mortgage and school costs before tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2036 I'll be 53, our younger child nineteen and our older twenty-five. I cannot guess their wages or whether either lives at home. Caption thinking work faces AGI in 2036, while capable robots could handle physical bicycle repairs around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my company for a dated plan for human emergency escalation and paid jobs as captions change. I'd tell Harun that the shop's paid bookings and parts costs belong on separate lines in our household budget. I'd tell viewers where to report a missing caption during an event.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade could let us reduce the mortgage and see whether the repair shop can take more customers, if both incomes continue. I would still expect my caption manager post to change or end in 2036, and I cannot treat Harun's physical trade as safe after 2039. Our children's future wages are not part of my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next year I'll keep a monthly record of additional paid shop repairs and parts costs without buying a second stand from our three-month reserve. I'll put 200 monthly toward mortgage principal only after school costs and cash reserve are protected, stopping if Harun's net repair income falls. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'll apply for posted local paid work only if the wage with Harun's confirmed net receipts covers our bills; if no offer works, I'll use our reserve for the search and take extra repair orders only while paying customers still book them.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the caption desk's future, but I can use the years to reduce debt and find out what customers actually pay. I don't need a second repair stand to write down a number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger will be nineteen and the older twenty-five. I have no idea what either will earn, and I will not set a mortgage payment around their future money. Our plan uses wages that actually arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why avoid a second stand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stand has a price even on a day when no one books a repair. If the receipts show enough extra demand, we could consider it later after cash is safe. My partner Harun's bicycle shop is a business, not a spare salary in our cupboard.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I expect the caption manager wage to disappear while Harun's bicycle repair pay alone cannot meet the mortgage. A written staffing date, proof that extra bicycle bookings pay after parts, a real affordable job offer and a way to report missing emergency captions would help. Three months saved gives us time to ask, not time to stop earning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the deaf viewer whether a perfect-looking caption arrived before the important word was spoken. Silence can have excellent punctuation. A person in the room still needs to know what the audience received.

portrait: Zoe, **43**, leads seven live-caption editors at a large media company and holds an MBA.
She uses AI **occasionally after listening** to the feed and has strong judgment when events change suddenly.
Her typical manager pay, Harun's bicycle repairs and **three months cash** support two children and a mortgage.
She tests **extra booked shop work** while counting net receipts and keeping AGI and robot dates separate.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her caption manager wage before her household has a new affordable income.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **extra paid bicycle bookings** that add net income beyond Harun's existing work.
She needs **written staffing terms**, an affordable job offer and emergency caption escalation.
